newsitem.title: UK: UK M4 strong, but retail sales hold key to rates.
newsitem.headline: UK M4 strong, but retail sales hold key to rates.

text.p: A strong rise in M4 money supply in June suggests strong high street activity in the month, but analysts say retail sales data on Wednesday will be crucial in determining the timing of the next interest rate rise.
"It looks like people who have received windfall cash have put it into bank and building society accounts," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers.
"But what we really need to know is if it is going to stay there, or is it only a temporary measure before it is spent on cars and holidays."
M4 money supply grew by 11.6 percent in the year to June compared with 11.1 percent in the year to May, while M4 lending was 5.5 billion pounds compared with 9.1 billion in May.
June retail sales figures, due on Wednesday, will be crucial in determining how much of the windfall cash is leaking into the economy.

In May, retail sales rose by 1.1 percent in the month, leading to speculation that consumers were spending more in advance of windfall payments from building societies due to change to banks and float on the stock market.
The Bank said strong growth in M4 was one of the factors it took into account when it raised rates to 6.75 percent from 6.5 last Thursday.
In a statement accompanying the rate rise it said monetary growth, along with other key indicators, made the rise necessary.

"It concluded that the latest month's evidence -- notably the upward revision of estimated output growth in the fourth quarter of 1996 and recent developments in monetary growth and retail sales -- indicated that a further tightening of monetary policy was necessary..." it said.
But economists on Friday said they did not think June's M4 data would have much of an impact on the Bank's thinking when it meets on August 6 and 7.
"I don't think today's figure will sway the Bank one way or the other on rates," said Nick Parsons, strategist at Paribas Capital Markets.

"It doesn't really shed any fresh light on the debate. The key thing for policy will be consumer spending and the breakdown over the next four weeks. If that slows, the Bank may hold off at the next meeting."
M4 has lost much of its reputation as a leading indicator of inflation and has been above the government's monitoring range of three to nine percent for 21 months in succession.

In recent months it has been swollen by activity in the gilt repo market. Last month, activity in that market helped to push M4 growth up by 1.4 percent on the month and M4 lending to 9.1 billion stg.
June's data showed a reversal of this repo activity which allowed M4 growth and lending to ease.
M4 lending was 5.5 billion pounds in June.
"We were looking for a big drop in gilt repos and got only a moderate payback. Perhaps the worrying thing is we had the drop in repos and still got a strong number," said Dicks.
In June, the change in gilt repos included in M4 was -4.2 billion stg, the Bank said. The change in reverse repos included in M4 lending was 600, millions pounds in June.
Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica, said the relatively modest rise in M4 lending would reassure those who fear the consumer sector has embarked on a runaway boom.
But the high level of personal borrowing will not do much to dampen speculation of higher interest rates during the summer.
"Lending to the personal sector was strong, so speculation about a Bank of England rate hike next month will persist. Our bet is the base rate will hit seven percent in September."

Figures from the British Bankers' Association showed consumer borrowing was buoyant in June, rising by 526 million stg compared with May's 595 million rise. The six-monthly average is 469 million stg.
